title: why are there no ai one-shotting hoi-like games?
author: Novel_Cucumber_1588
selftext:
as a fan of hoi, victoria games by paradox interactive,

after seeing all those "astra made this awesome 3d looking game in one shot lol" hype posts,

  
it just got me wondering "okay great. but why are there no strategic focused games being one shotted?"

these games aren't that awesome graphic demanding.

the core is making the economy, warfare, resource interaction algorithms and computation optimization which seems like an area that ai would just kick-ass.



any attempt that matches current paradox interactive's products or show that it can make this much more entertaining/realistic/interesting in some parts  would be just mind blowing

  
would love to see people throwing astra tokens in this direction.

comments.author: pixelfoundrystudios
comments.body: One shotting is not an effective way to make a game, particularly a complex system of economics and politics. HOI is nothing if not complex.

comments.author: Baraga91
comments.body:
I have some basic core game loop prototypes laying around, and let me tell you: the old adage is 100% true, graphics basically are a sideshow in game development. 

The key question for every project is "is the core game loop fun?", and it's beyond difficult to make a HOI-competitor that offers something different AND is fun. Yes, AI offers a lot of the benefits you mentioned, but the one thing it has 0 grasp of is whether or not people will actually like playing it. 

Just my 2c, but it's something to keep in mind :)

replies.author: pixelfoundrystudios
replies.body: You sound like you have a good grasp on the subject. I’m curious what you’re building?

replies.author: Baraga91
replies.body:
At this point I have a football (soccer) league prediction game in open beta (a simple web app inspired by my newfound interest after the world cup :p ) and a space exploration game that I'm actively building (it's based on old school space lander games, but with a real story line and a progressively more complex and expanding world).

Aside from that, there are like a dozen minor projects ranging from rough drafts to even rougher prototypes on my hard drive, that are basically ideas that needed a place to go :)

comments.author: SimCFB
comments.body:
The games you see one shotted are like very tiny slivers. They look impressive as a demo. But fail completely as a full game because they lack any depth.

A lot of these games don't have a ton of depth to begin with. And even then there is not enough to make a full game.

What you're talking about is some of the deepest games ever made. Of course it's impossible to one shot it. You'd end up with completely useless slop.

Now is it possible to build a game like that with codex? Yes of course. But you won't one shot it. It will take many long hours of fine tuning and prompting.

replies.author: Kindly-Sail6260
replies.body: I notice they generally fail as a demo too since most of the people making them don’t have any understanding on what a demo actually looks like. The majority I see are mostly alpha builds like God of War when it was a gray box and Kratos looks so low res but with colors slapped on it and it’s a “game”. We definitely need to raise the bar on what we find actually impressive than being impressed that AI can do it. We know AI can do it. Now make a real game 🦧

comments.author: BlueAndYellowTowels
comments.body:
I'm currently in the early stage of building a 4x game. Because that's my favorite genre. 

The reason you don't see a one-shot of a game like that is it requires a LOT more explanation and iteration. You can't just "one shot" a game like Civilization 6 or Stellaris. That's not happening. You have have prototype out the basic loop, get a feel for the mechanics and then keep expanding on the systems.

In my instance, I even had Astra refactor their code to make certain parts generic so it could easily accept new options and configurations where needed.

Like, I spent, maybe 10 hours... and I've barely fleshed out the core loop... because it requires a lot of time to think about and test to see if that "feels" right.

Because there's no physics or cinematics doing the lifting for the player, you really need tight systems to to work.

...and that's just the prototype. Nevermind then scaling out it out to AI opponents and then thousands of squares, hexes, provinces... whatever... 

This is why I personally was excited about Astra and AI game dev. Because 4x games tend to be very complex and they require teams. But, with Astra I feel like the workload has shrunk a bit so that now, a single person could potentially bring a strategy game like HoI or Civ together with some effort and vision.

...and Astra is up to the task. I added some mechanics I've never seen in a 4x game to my prototype and then I kind of played with it a bit to see. I dialed it in by having Astra make some changes here and there... it feels really good now and adds a really nice strategic layer to the game. I'm excited to see how much father it goes.

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
I think that one of the reason they might be extra challenging, is because there is tons of manual tweaking involved. And tons of playtesting, imagination, balancing etc.  
  
It has to nail down a very delicate balance. It has to decide where to have complexity and where to avoid it.  
Put to much complexity into something player hates and considers "stupid busy work"- and the game sucks.   
Put too little complexity - and player is figuring it out too fast and is bored.

It just boils down to the fact, that you gonna need to write a small book of a prompts to create a 4x game that is not outright garbage.

Even for a full fledged game from a big developer - some of their vanilla, pre-expansion games were really meh, and took like 3 expansions in order not to suck.

If it takes so much efforts for a company that has so much experience, I can\`t imagine it being much easier for solo-AI assisted dev...
